claim: The Jews left 2,000 years ago and came back as Europeans.

answer: Jews went from a majority in the first century to a minority by the fifth: one source says most dispersed after the Roman wars, another accepts about 580,000 Jewish dead in 132-135. Jews were about 13,000 of 340,000 people in 1850, and a tiny minority in 1917. But not all left: after 135 the centre of Jewish life moved to the Galilee, where the Jerusalem Talmud was compiled about 400. Jewish communities are recorded under Byzantine, early Islamic, Crusader, Mamluk and Ottoman rule, above all Safed in the 16th century. Jerusalem had almost no Jews in 1267. By the 1850s to 1860s Jews were the largest single group in Jerusalem. By the Central Bureau of Statistics (own or father's birthplace), 28% of Israel's Jews in 2021 were of European or American origin and 22% of Asian or African; a survey tracing grandparents found 45% Mizrahi and 32% Ashkenazi.

facts.text: After the Roman wars (70 and 132-135 CE) the centre of Jewish life moved north to the Galilee, where the Jerusalem Talmud, produced in the Galilean academies (above all Tiberias), was compiled about 400 CE; the Mishnah dates to about 200 CE.

facts.text: Under Byzantine and then early Muslim rule Jews remained in the land: Jews controlled the mainly Jewish towns of the Galilee, Tiberias stayed the capital of the Jews in the country until the religious authorities moved to Jerusalem after the Arab conquest of the 630s, and a rabbinic academy later worked in Tiberias and Ramle.

sources.title: Under Byzantine Christianity
sources.quote: the patriarchate and the Sanhedrin were officially recognized, and Jews controlled those municipalities in the Galilee which were primarily Jewish

facts.text: In the Mamluk period (1260-1517) Jewish communities existed in Safed, Jerusalem and Hebron, though Jerusalem had almost no Jews when Nachmanides arrived in 1267 and the city's Jews numbered only about seventy families in 1488.

facts.text: After 1099 the Crusaders did not permit Jews to live in Jerusalem (the ban on a Jew's entry was strictly enforced in the early decades), though they could live elsewhere in Palestine and some settled near the citadel by Benjamin of Tudela's visit.

sources.title: Jerusalem
sources.quote: Muslims and Jews were not permitted to reside in the city; however, the Muslims came into the city for business purposes and some Jews settled near the citadel.

facts.text: In the 16th century Ottoman tax registers record a growing Jewish community in Safed (232 Jewish families in 1525-26, 716 Jewish households in 1548), where Joseph Karo and Isaac Luria worked; Jewish communities also grew in Jerusalem, Tiberias, Hebron and elsewhere.

facts.text: In the mid-19th century, before political Zionism (first Zionist Congress, 1897), Jews were the largest single group in Jerusalem: Karl Marx reported 8,000 Jews among 15,500 'sedentary' inhabitants in 1854; the British consul's 1865 report gave 8,000-9,000 Jews among about 18,000; the 1868 Jerusalem Almanack gave 9,000 Jews, 5,000 Muslims and 4,000 Christians.

facts.text: Jews fell from a majority of the land's population to a minority over the first centuries of the Common Era. Sergio DellaPergola's rough estimates show a Jewish majority in the first century and a Christian majority from the 2nd to the 6th centuries; the Center for Online Judaic Studies says the Jews of Palestine were already a minority in their own land under Constantine and that Christians became the majority in the fifth century. Neither says how much of the fall was death, flight or conversion.

facts.text: Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics classes Jews by their own or their father's continent of birth: of 6.98 million Jews at the end of 2021, 9.1% were of Asian origin, 12.7% of African origin, 28.3% of Europe-America and 49.8% of Israeli origin (father born in Israel). In a survey that traces grandparents' birthplace, Mizrahi Jews (from Asia and North Africa) were 44.9% and Ashkenazi 31.8%; Pew found Israeli Jews roughly evenly divided between Ashkenazi and Sephardi or Mizrahi identity; The Conversation gives about 40% to 45% Mizrahi and 32% Ashkenazi, as shares of the whole population (Jews and non-Jews), so its shares are not comparable with the survey's shares of Jews.

facts.text: After the revolts against Rome, conditions convinced most Jewish residents to disperse, according to My Jewish Learning, which adds that no decree ordered them to leave; an archaeological study (Raviv, 2021) judges Cassius Dio's figure of 580,000 Jewish victims of the Bar Kokhba war (132-135) a reasonable account of the total. The two sources describe different things (dispersal; deaths) and do not say how they divide.

contested.text: Whether Jews were a majority or a plurality of Jerusalem in the 1860s is disputed. The Encyclopaedia Judaica says they became a majority 'for the first time in 1800 years' in the mid-1860s, but the consul's count it cites (8,000-9,000 of 18,000) is about half; Jewish Virtual Library's table gives the Jewish share as 46% in 1844 and 48% in 1876; Teach Jewish History says a majority by about 1880 and that Ottoman registers counted fewer Jews.

sources.title: Jerusalem
sources.quote: in the middle years of the decade the Jews became a majority in the city for the first time in 1800 years.

sources.title: Demographics of Israel: Population of Jerusalem (1844-present)
The Continuous Jewish Presence in the Land
sources.quote: Jerusalem (the city, not the wider territory) had a Jewish majority by about 1880, according to consular and travelers' estimates (Ottoman registers, kept mainly for taxes and incomplete, counted fewer Jews).

contested.text: How continuous the Jewish presence was is argued. Michael Ehrlich writes that Jerusalem had no Jewish community when the Mamluks took it, and Nachmanides's 1267 letter, which the same article quotes, found only two Jewish brothers there. Jewish presence is documented in every period, but it thinned and was rebuilt by immigrants.

contested.text: The 'no mass exile' position holds that the Romans did not deport the Jews of Judea, that many Judeans stayed, converted over the centuries to Christianity and then Islam, and are among the ancestors of today's Palestinians. Shlomo Sand argues this and says the early Zionists believed it; he cites Yitzhak Ben-Zvi, later Israel's second president, writing in 1929 that the peasant farmers came largely from earlier Jewish farmers. Population-genetics reviews report that Jewish populations of Europe, North Africa and the Middle East form a cluster distinct from their non-Jewish neighbours, with Palestinians among the nearest non-Jewish neighbours, and that Khazar admixture in Ashkenazi Jews is speculative. Sand's position here is taken from an interview (Consortium News) and a review of his book (AlterNet), not from his book. The historian Robert Wistrich, reviewing Sand in The Jerusalem Post, wrote that Sand 'has failed to demolish the myths on which the history of the Jewish people has been constructed' (a headline summary; the review text was not readable).

could_not_verify: Sources saying that most Jews outside the land outnumbered those in it, century by century: none read; the card says only that most Jewish residents dispersed after the revolts (My Jewish Learning) and gives population shares.
Dated evidence for Hebron's Jewish community through the centuries on three independent readable pages: only Encyclopaedia Judaica and Teach Jewish History (advocacy) were readable.
The source of the Prussian consul's 1845 count (about 7,000 Jews of about 16,000): not found on a readable independent page.

Sand's own book: only an interview (Consortium News) and a review (AlterNet) were read. The only historian quoted against his thesis is Wistrich, from the standfirst of a review whose text was not readable; Israel Bartal's reply is in Haaretz behind a paywall.

A source stating why Jews became a minority: the third source for that fact (Raviv) concerns the Bar Kokhba casualties only; scholarship tying the decline to the Byzantine period was not found in a quotable page.

Three independent sources for each of: Jews a majority in the 1st century and a minority by the 5th (now DellaPergola and COJS, two); most Jewish residents dispersed after the revolts (only My Jewish Learning); Jewish dead in 132-135 (only Raviv). Fact 6 is now split so each claim stands on its own sources: fact 6 (the shift to a minority) has two reliable sources, fact 9 (dispersal, and the 580,000 dead) has two, one for each clause. A person should read a scholarly history of Roman and Byzantine Palestine (for example Schwartz, Imperialism and Jewish Society, or Cambridge's Jews in Late Antiquity) for each clause.

The Israeli Central Bureau of Statistics table on origin (fact 7) is read as a government source; the three reliable sources on that fact report survey and census data on ethnic origin, not the same CBS figures, so it is not reworded as a record fact. A person should look for a reliable reader of CBS table 2.9.
The McCarthy figures for 1850-51 and 1914-15 (fact 8) are his corrected estimates from Ottoman registers, which were not read; the fact is attributed to him and to Khalidi.
not_claimed: That Jewish presence gives Jews a right to the land or settles any modern political question.
That the Jewish population was large or continuous at every time or place: it was small, interrupted, and refreshed by immigration from Spain, North Africa and Europe.

That Ashkenazi immigration of the 19th and 20th centuries did not happen: 28% of Israel's Jews were of European or American origin in 2021 by the Central Bureau of Statistics' classification, and 31.8% were Ashkenazi in one survey.
That Arabs and Muslims were not the large majority of the land's people: see the Arab and Muslim presence card.

answer_claims.says: Jews went from a majority in the first century to a minority by the fifth: one source says most dispersed after the Roman wars, another accepts about 580,000 Jewish dead in 132-135.
Jews were about 13,000 of 340,000 people in 1850, and a tiny minority in 1917.
But not all left: after 135 the centre of Jewish life moved to the Galilee, where the Jerusalem Talmud was compiled about 400.
Jewish communities are recorded under Byzantine, early Islamic, Crusader, Mamluk and Ottoman rule, above all Safed in the 16th century.
Jerusalem had almost no Jews in 1267.
By the 1850s to 1860s Jews were the largest single group in Jerusalem.

By the Central Bureau of Statistics (own or father's birthplace), 28% of Israel's Jews in 2021 were of European or American origin and 22% of Asian or African; a survey tracing grandparents found 45% Mizrahi and 32% Ashkenazi.

skeptic.notes: ROUND THREE. Fact 6 re-read against its four quotes: DellaPergola's text and table support only 'Jewish majority in the 1st century, Christian majority 2nd-6th'; My Jewish Learning supports 'most residents dispersed' (its page adds no decree to leave was given); Raviv supports only that Dio's 580,000 is a reasonable total of Jewish dead in 132-135 (he puts Judea's population at 500,000-650,000). So each clause has one source, and Raviv's figure points to death, not dispersal. The sentence as worded did not carry; I reworded the fact and the answer to what each source says and added that none says how the decline divided between death, flight and conversion. The gate's three-site count is a floor and is not met in substance, so fact 6 is marked thin and not verified. Wistrich's quote is from a review standfirst (the card says so) and Sand is read through an interview and a review (the card says so; the answer does not use Sand). Other facts unchanged from round two. Strongest objection from a Palestinian reader: the card still has no scholar saying Judeans stayed and converted beyond a press interview. From a Jewish reader: 'majority to minority by the fifth century' rests on one demographer's rough estimate.
